entries.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy says Patriot missile shortage costs lives
entries.summary: At least nine people died, and more than 20 were injured after Russia struck Ukraine's capital with ballistic missiles. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blames a lack of interceptor missiles for the deaths.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Zelenskyy says Patriot missile shortage costs lives

August 1, 2026

At least nine people died, and more than 20 were injured after Russia struck Ukraine's capital with ballistic missiles. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blames a lack of interceptor missiles for the deaths.

At least nine people died and 23 were injured after Russia struck Ukraine's capital city Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on Saturday morning.

The missiles struck several homes and a five-storey residential building, while cars were also set alight.

Four children were among the 23 injured, the emergency service said.

In a post on his Telegram account, Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said that several people were trapped in a damaged residential building during the attack.

The first and second floors of the building had partially collapsed, he said, while some warehouses in the city were also on fire.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched 35 missiles overnight, including 27 ballistic missiles, as well as 185 attack drones. He said only one ballistic missile was intercepted, blaming a shortage of interceptors for Ukraine's Patriot air defense systems.

"As usual, the Russians struck ordinary residential buildings," Zelenskyy said, adding that 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy and infrastructure facilities were damaged.

"Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people," he said. "And every night without them results in more casualties."

The attacks come as Moscow has intensified its bombing campaigns in recent weeks and months.

Last week,Zelenskyy met with his US counterpart Donald Trump and the UK's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham as he seeks increased support to boost Ukraine's air defences.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: India: Modi says he forgives 'children' who abused him
entries.summary: Modi shared a video message in which he described CJP protesters as "misguided children" who deserve guidance.
entries.content:
Asia

India: Modi says he forgives 'children' who abused him

August 1, 2026

Modi shared a video message in which he described CJP protesters as "misguided children" who deserve guidance.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared a video message on Friday night in which he said he is forgiving students who hurled abuses at him during the Cockroach Janta Party protests at Jantar Mantar in Delhi last month.

The protests, ignited by an exam paper leak, snowballed into what is considered the biggest challenge to Modi's rule to date, culminating with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

What did Modi say about the Cockroach protesters?

Modi described the protesters as "misguided children" who deserve guidance rather than punishment or prolonged legal action.

In the video message, he said the language used by some protesters "would not suit any civilized society."

"Some mischievous children used very filthy abuses... Abuses were directed at me, and abuses were directed at my late mother as well," Modi said.

"These are misguided children, and showing them the way is our duty," he said.

He added that punishing them or making them "run around courts" was not going to change the circumstances. "I want to forgive them, and society too should accept this."

"Children, come, let us move forward together for the country," Modi went on to say. "Let us learn something new, let us learn even from mistakes... I live for you, I toil for your bright future, so come, let us together take the country forward."

Girl reported for using abusive language against Modi

The video message by Modi came on the same day as police received a report regarding a viral video showing a woman allegedly using abusive language against the prime minister during the recent Jantar Mantar protest.

The girl in the video has apologised for her remarks, as reported by Indian newspaper Hindustan Times.

In a video message, she said, "I came under the influence of some people at the protest and said a lot of bad things against the Prime Minister," according to Indian media reports.

The police report identifies the girl as 25 years old. However, in the apology video, she said she is "just 15 years old."

Meanwhile, the CJP has questioned the incident.

"Since when has using abusive language become a criminal offense in this country?" CJP spokesperson Saurav Das asked, claiming that 50% of the MPs face criminal charges, yet no action is taken against them.

He alleged that police reports in such cases are being filed to "single out" people and "make an example of them."

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Germany news: Pride marches planned after Berlin attack
entries.summary: Several German cities are holding Pride events a week after a deadly attack on a march in Berlin. A forest fire is burning out of control in Bavaria. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Pride marches planned after Berlin attack

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 1, 2026

Several German cities are holding Pride events a week after a deadly attack on a march in Berlin. A forest fire is burning out of control in Bavaria. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Pride events are to take place in several German cities a week after a deadly attack on a Pride march in Berlin
  • Authorities warn of holiday traffic disruption in Germany amid the two-hour closure of a key pass road in Austria
  • A forest fire is burning out of control in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria

Here is a round-up of some of the main stories from and about Germany hitting the headlines on Saturday, August 1, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Forest fire breaks out in Bavaria

Forest fire breaks out in Bavaria

Some 330 emergency personnel have been deployed to fight a forest fire that broke out on Friday near Freudenberg in the Upper Palatinate region of Bavaria.

The fire is burning out of control in difficult terrain amid strong winds, local authorities said, with a thunderstorm hampering firefighting operations.

People have been warned to avoid the area, while authorities have advised residents to keep windows and doors closed, turn off air conditioning and ventilation systems and follow local radio for further information.

Europe as a whole has seen several major blazes so far this seasonas human-induced climate change increasingly produces conditions conducive to their ignition.

Skip next section Train punctuality still 'not good' in first half of 2026 — DB head

Train punctuality still 'not good' in first half of 2026 — DB head

Just 58.7% of Germany's long-distance trains arrived on time at their destination in the first half of the year, with the head of national rail operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) conceding that there was much room for improvement.

"That is not a good figure. There's no point trying to gloss over it," Evelyn Palla told the Sunday edition of the Welt newspaper.

However, Palla, who took over as head of DB in October 2025, said the delay was less than 15 minutes in three-quarters of the cases.

"Even though we are not yet satisfied overall, we should not make Deutsche Bahn out to be worse than it is," she said.

DB considers a long-distance train delayed if it arrives at least six minutes late, with canceled trains included in the company's operational punctuality statistics.

Palla had set a punctuality target of at least 60% for this year and has worked to streamline the company by cutting several management positions, among other things.

DB has also begun to overhaul key lines as it seeks to improve its services, which have long been the object of criticism from those who rely on them. 

Skip next section Storms leave 1 dead in Saxony, cause disruption in Hamburg

Storms leave 1 dead in Saxony, cause disruption in Hamburg

A severe storm has hit the Saxon Switzerland region in the eastern state of Saxony, with a 28-year-old man killed by a falling tree, police said on Friday.

A number of other people were also injured, some seriously, amid the bad weather, they said.

The fatality occurred near the Felsenbühne open-air theater in the town of Rathen on Friday evening.

A performance of the musical "Little Shop of Horrors" at the theater, one of the largest open-air theaters in Saxony, was cancelled.

Parts of the Saxon Switzerland national park was closed to visitors on Saturday, with authorities saying there was still a risk from falling trees.

Germany's national meteorological service, the DWD, had issued warnings about severe thunderstorms for large parts of Saxony, saying there could be possible lightning strikes, falling trees and flying debris.

Meanwhile, a severe storm also swept the northern port city of Hamburg on Friday evening, with the fire brigade responding to almost 100 call-outs.

Most were water-related incidents.

No injuries were reported amid the storm, which was reported to have particularly affected the southern and northern outskirts of the city.

Skip next section Traffic disruption expected as Austrian pass road blocked

Traffic disruption expected as Austrian pass road blocked

Austria's Fern Pass road is to be closed for some two hours on Saturday morning amid a demonstration, with authorities warning of delays to holiday traffic as vacations get underway in Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

The road is a key north-south transit route linking Germany, Austria and Italy.

Protesters are demonstrating not only at the volume of traffic on the route but also against a planned tunnel intended to replace the most difficult section of the road.

They say the project will only attract more traffic.

The nearby Hahntennjoch Pass will also be temporarily closed amid the protest, which is expected to be attended by hundreds of people.

The Fern Pass, which reaches an elevation of 1,212 meters (almost 4,000 feet), carries more traffic than almost any other pass in the eastern Alps, second only to the Brenner Pass.

Skip next section Pride events planned in several German cities after attack

Pride events planned in several German cities after attack

Pride events in several German cities are expected to draw hundreds of thousands of people on Saturday.

The events are to take place just a week after a man rammed a car into the Berlin Pride march, killing a woman and injuring 31 other people.German authorities said they were treating the incident as an "Islamist terrorist attack." The suspect was later shot dead by German police as they tried to arrest him.

In Hamburg, where some 250,000 people are expected to gather, police have announced that they will deploy twice as many officers as last year to protect the event.

The march is expected to feature a float from the Berlin organizers on which participants will wear dark clothing in tribute to the victims.

Pride events are also planned in the cities of Bonn, Ahaus and Moers in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, and another in the eastern city of Naumburg in Saxony-Anhalt.

In Germany, such events are called Christopher Street Day (CSD) in commemoration of events in New York in 1969 after police raided the Stonewall Inn bar on Christopher Street.

The raids triggered days of protests by gay, lesbian and transgender people that became the starting point for a worldwide rights movement.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn says guten Tag to all its readers as we get underway with our look-round at stories with a Germany slant on the first day of the month.

Topping the list are the planned Pride events scheduled to take place across the country amid heightened security after a deadly attack a week ago on a march in Berlin.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to turn out in support of the LGBTQ+ community and societal diversity.

The summer is also bringing its share of extreme weather events and fires to Germany, with severe storms in the north and east and a major blaze in a southern forest.

Join us here for these and other stories from Europe's biggest economy!

entries.title: FIFA chief Infantino abandons World Cup sell-off plans after backlash
entries.summary: Europe's governing body, UEFA, had threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup, unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his plans to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private equity investors.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

FIFA chief Infantino abandons World Cup sell-off plans

August 1, 2026

Europe's governing body, UEFA, had threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup, unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his plans to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private equity investors.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has withdrawn his plans to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors.

Infantino's plans had been met with widespread condemnation from across the football world.

In a statement on Saturday, Infantino said: "Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."

What were FIFA chief's Infantino's private investor plans?

Infantino's proposal would have created a commercial subsidiary, the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run competitions like the World Cup, selling broadcasting and sponsorship, tickets and hospitality.

Under the plans, FIFA would sell minority stakes in FFE to private equity investors. The proposed investor consortium was to be led by "Thrive Eternal," a fund run by "Thrive Capital," which was founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US ​President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Infantino, who has faced criticism for his close ties to the US president, had asked federations to approve the measure by September 19, reportedly offering the associations $40 million (€35 million) if they backed the proposal.

Infantino's plans met with global backlash

UEFA, the governing body of European football, said on Thursday that its members had unanimously agreed to boycott all FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup, unless the plan was withdrawn.

"The World Cup is not for sale," UEFA said.

European teams are the reigning champions of FIFA's three leading competitions, the men's and women's World Cup, and the Club World Cup.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and CONCACAF, which runs the sport in North America and the Caribbean, soon joined UEFA in condemning and rejecting FIFA's plans, although they stopped short of threatening a boycott.

As the opposition to Infantino's plans grew, his senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigned in protest on Friday.

Later on Friday, the world governing body's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, slammed Infantino, saying the plans were "the project of one person" who had "deceived" FIFA staff.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak becomes world's second-largest ever
entries.summary: DR Congo’s fast-spreading Ebola outbreak has exceeded 3,500 cases, overtaking the country’s deadliest epidemic and becoming the world’s second-largest ever. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment.
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

DR Congo’s fast-spreading Ebola outbreak has exceeded 3,500 cases, overtaking the country’s deadliest epidemic and becoming the world’s second-largest ever. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment.

The Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) latest Ebola outbreak has surpassed the total number of cases recorded during the country's deadliest epidemic between 2018 and 2020.

That epidemic killed nearly 2,300 people among about 3,500 infections.

Congolese officials said on Friday that in this year's outbreak 3,532 Ebola cases, including 1,556 deaths, have now been confirmed across five provinces.

Second-Largest Ebola Outbreak on Record

The outbreak has grown into the world's second-largest Ebola epidemic.

"It's the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic that we have ever seen," said Carl Skau, acting executive director of the UN World Food Programme told ​Reuters.

"The world needs to pay much more attention," he added.

The outbreak has proven unusually deadly, killing five times more people in its first three months than previous Ebola outbreaks had by the same stage, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Only the 2014-16 West Africa outbreak was bigger, with 28,616 cases reported across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Ebolais a severe and often fatal disease that spreads from infected animals and through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.

Experimental vaccines raise hope

The outbreak is being caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which no approved vaccine or treatment currently exists.

However, vaccine research is gaining momentum — the WHO has described a vaccine being developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories as the most promising candidate against the outbreak.

A separate Bundibugyo vaccine is also under development by the University of Oxford. Last week, the first volunteer received a dose as part of an ongoing clinical trial.

Ebola Spreads Amid Conflict and Instability

The outbreak is centred in Ituri province in northeastern DR Congo, near the borders with South Sudan and Uganda.

Health officials say the true scale of the epidemic remains unclear.

Since the outbreak was declared, cases have risen rapidly. Confirmed infections increased from 2,000 on July 15 to more than 3,500 within weeks.

The virus has also spread to four other provinces. These include North Kivu and South Kivu, where large areas are controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group.

DR Congo is grappling with ongoing instability in its eastern regions, where conflict involving the M23 rebel group continues despite peace efforts.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: UK court allows plans for Chinese 'super' embassy to advance
entries.summary: A court dismissed a legal challenge against Beijing's new embassy in London, which could become the largest in the UK. The case, brought by a neighborhood association, argued the embassy poses a security threat.
entries.content:
China

UK court allows plans for Chinese 'super' embassy to advance

July 31, 2026

A court dismissed a legal challenge against Beijing's new embassy in London, which could become the largest in the UK. The case, brought by a neighborhood association, argued the embassy poses a security threat.

A UK High Court on Friday threw out a challenge against UK authorities' decision to permit a new Chinese super embassy in central London.

The challenge was brought by a neighborhood group called the Royal Mint Court Residents' Association (RMCRA), which represents families and businesses in roughly 100 properties around the planned embassy site.

What was the court case about?

The RMCRA argued the presence of the embassy could increase the risk of terrorist attacks, lead to the targeting of dissidents and be used to enforce "draconian" Chinese laws in the UK.

The association also claimed that the embassy could pose a fire risk, arguing that Chinese authorities might ignore safety obligations that would be difficult to enforce because of diplomatic immunity on the embassy site.

On that basis, the group argued the development should not have been approved by the UK government as well as the London Borough of Tower Hamlets.

Yet in its ruling on Friday, the High Court said the "RMCRA ​did not produce reasonable ⁠and convincing evidence of the likelihood that a violation of human rights ⁠affecting them ​personally would occur."

In a move that was widely seen as a goodwill gesture toward Beijing, the embassy received approval from the UK government shortly before then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer visited China in January this year. 

What makes a 'super embassy'?

 If completed, the new Chinese embassy would be the largest embassy in the UK.

Beijing plans to build the embassy on the site of the former Royal Mint, next to the Tower of London. The site covers around 20,000 square meters (235,000 square feet).

Beijing purchased the property in 2018 for a reported $327 million (€283.9 million), with the intent of relocating its embassy there from its current premises in Portland Place.

RMCRA vows to continue fight

In response to the verdict, the RMCRA said it would seek permission to appeal, hoping to take the case to the UK Supreme Court.

"Beijing thinks this judgment is the final word. It isn't. The appeal is already in the works," Luke Pollard, head of the RMCRA, said in a statement.

Opposition to the project extends far beyond local residents.

Activists from Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement living in exile have also been skeptical of the project, telling DW they fear the embassy could help Beijing suppress dissidents abroad. 

The UK is home to the world's largest Hong Kong diaspora, with an estimated 285,000 people of Hong Kong origin living in the country.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Why Europe's wildfires are getting harder to stop
entries.summary: Wildfires may start with a single spark, but experts say climate change, drought and decades of forest management decisions have created the conditions for Europe's biggest blazes.
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

Wildfires may start with a single spark, but experts say climate change, drought and decades of forest management decisions have created the conditions for Europe's biggest blazes.

Wildfires almost always need a spark to ignite, whether it's lightning, arson, or a car's hot exhaust pipe touching dry vegetation.

In France's historic summer wildfires, authorities blamed a brush-clearing machine being operated around a high-voltage power line. Spanish investigators concluded that sparks from heavy machinery were behind major blazes there.

But scientists say those findings only explain how Europe's historic wildfires began, not why they grew into the megafires that have devastated the continent this summer.

Across Europe, a combination of human-caused climate change, insufficient planning and forests planted in ways that allow flames to spread quickly are fueling fires, say experts.

"It's not that wildfires are magic and just start. You have to have the right climatic conditions," said Silvia Abruscato, coordinator of FoRISK, a pan-European forest risk management hub.

Climate change is loading forests with fuel

Scientists point to three ingredients that determine whether a wildfire will spread rapidly: the amount of vegetation available to burn, how dry that vegetation is, and the weather conditions around a fire.

"When all three of these conditions are very much fire-prone and they align, then you have this kind of fire event," said Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.

Climate change is making these conditions more common and intense. A rapid analysisfrom World Weather Attribution found global warming made the extreme weather behind Spain and France's summer wildfires much more likely.   

One reason is a phenomenon called hydroclimatic whiplash, where ecosystems suddenly swing between wet and dry conditions.

Essentially, as the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, intensifying rainfall that fuels plant growth.

"This has created an abundance of biomass that then has rapidly dried during a sequence of heat waves," Di Giuseppe said.

In spring, a warmer atmosphere draws water from soil and plants. Drought worsens, vegetation dries out, and landscapes become far easier to ignite. In simple terms, wet winters grow fuel, and dry springs turn that fuel into perfect kindling.

This summer, that's meant fires breaking out almost simultaneously in France, Spain, Greece, and Turkey — all driven by the same broad pattern of heat and drought.

Making matters worse, the fires themselves add to the problem. This year's blazes have already emitted nearly 18 million tons of planet-warming CO2, according to EU figures.

Some forests are built to burn

Once a fire begins, it can take thousands of firefighters days or weeks of effort to contain the flames. That's partly due to the way forests have been managed over decades. Across parts of Europe, large areas have been planted as monocultures, dominated by a single species grown for quick timber. 

"Some of the fires we've been seeing in France and Spain are in places where you have these very flammable trees which are quite fine and they often are growing close together so fire spreads really easily," Doug Kelley, a land surface modeler at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, told DW.

More than three-quarters of the Landes de Gascogne forest in southwestern France, which is currently ablaze, contains maritime pine. Created after Napoleon III ordered the region's marshes to be drained and planted with pine in 1857, it became Europe's largest man-made forest.

But the pine species sheds coarse needles that blanket the forest floor, providing bountiful fuel for fires. Because the trees are of similar age and height across vast areas, they are particularly vulnerable to fast-moving fire.

Another fast-growing timber tree is the eucalyptus. In Portugal the oily species — which represents more than a quarter of the country's forestland — burned far and wide in 2017's deadly wildfire season.

"In some regions of Europe, farmland and lower-biomass shrubland were replaced by fire-prone conifer or eucalyptus species of higher economic profitability, increasing the risk of fire," the European Commission wrote in a case study reporton the 2017 Portuguese wildfires.

That includes Spain, where some 3 million hectares (7.4 million acres) of former farmland and pasture were planted with pine and eucalyptus during and after the Franco dictatorship, which lasted from 1939 to 1975.

Preventing the next disaster

Firefighters will always play a crucial role in suppressing wildfires. But experts say reducing risk before fires start is just as important. That starts with tackling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change and intensifying weather extremes.

"Trying to prevent in the first place the landscape becoming so flammable is one of the most effective ways to try to avoid this kind of extreme fire behavior," said Di Giuseppe.

Replacing monocultures with mixed forests would also go a long way. Forests with a wider variety of species are generally better able to withstand drought, windstorms, insect outbreaks, and fires, because different trees respond differently to environmental stresses.

Germany offers an instructive case for forest management. Demand for timber after World War II led to spruce being planted across mountain ranges like the Harz in former East Germany. But these monocultures proved vulnerable to drought and bark beetle infestation. Foresters are now working to convert them into mixed forests to improve resilience.

Planting broadleaf, deciduous trees — such as oak, beech, or maple — can help, as they typically store more moisture than conifers. Trees with thick bark, fewer low-hanging branches, and a higher moisture content tend to be more fire-resistant.

A post-event simulation studyof Portugal's 2017 blazes found fires that overwhelmed firefighters in pine and eucalyptus stands, with flames over four meters tall, could be contained in broadleaf forest, where flame heights dropped to under a meter and a half.

Forestry experts also recommend creating breaks between rows of trees to slow fire spread as well as pruning lower branches so flames can't jump quickly to the canopy. Clearing the forest floor of incendiary leaf litter and dead wood, and using controlled burns to reduce underbrush prior to wildfire season helps too.

"We need to manage our forest well in order to avoid such big disasters from happening. So prevention, prevention, prevention," Abruscato said.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: Sudan civil war: When drones strike the classroom
entries.summary: Children in Sudan's besieged city of el-Obeid are afraid to go to school as drone attacks hit civilian infrastructure. Aid groups warn of a worsening humanitarian crisis.
entries.content:
Sudan

Sudan civil war: When drones strike the classroom

July 31, 2026

Children in Sudan's besieged city of el-Obeid are afraid to go to school as drone attacks hit civilian infrastructure. Aid groups warn of a worsening humanitarian crisis.

Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of el-Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet.

Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan.

The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, a native of el-Obeid and a project manager for children's rights organization Plan International there. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand people who are displaced — is under siege, he added.

There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long lines of people at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." Most of the time, children and teenagers are the ones sent to fetch water.

He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school.

"One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because they are always in fear of something happening again," he said.

Even when they're sitting in their classrooms, they live with the constant fear that a drone could strike at any moment. Awad and his colleagues at Plan International are working to provide psychological support to the affected children.

Sudan's strategic crossroads

El-Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF. 

El-Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure.

Warnings of mass atrocities

Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture el-Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of el-Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege.

Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of el-Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide."

“We warn that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of the horrific human rights violations and abuses against civilians that we documented in Al-Fashir,” numerous human rights organizations said in a joint appeal.

"We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN chief's personal envoy for Sudan, in June. "These are already affecting the civilians and disrupting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk."

Growing up under drones

The situation is particularly dire for the children trapped in el-Obeid, says Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of the children's charity Save the Children in Sudan. Drone attacks on schools and displacement camps have caused severe trauma.

Lanino recently visited the Tawila displacement camp near el-Fashir in Darfur, which was taken over by the RSF in October. There, he encountered children struggling to process what had happened to them.

"We met several children who refused to speak afterwards," Lanino said. Many found it difficult to understand why they had experienced such violence.

Lanino is concerned about the long-term impact of the conflict. "If these traumas are not addressed, they could seek revenge, because all this stress, all this trauma, could erupt in a new wave of violence."

Sudan's army has launched a new offensive in Kordofan from the capital, Khartoum, and says it has taken control of the 360-kilometer-long highway linking Omdurman, Khartoum's twin city, with el-Obeid.

SAF Chief of Staff Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan recently inspected the newly captured areas in North Kordofan by helicopter and congratulated his troops. The advance has reopened supply routes to SAF units in El Obeid.

Residents of the previously besieged city celebrated the arrival of army forces, as the immediate threat appears to have receded for now.

As they retreated, RSF fighters looted markets and villages in North Kordofan and committed human rights violations against local residents, according to the Sudan Tribune media platform.

Last Monday, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as "Hemeti," told commanders in the affected areas they no longer needed to wait for orders from the high command and could instead launch counteroffensives at their own discretion.

The move could lead to further attacks on civilians and additional looting.

This article was first published on July 24, 2026. It was updated on July 31, 2026.

entries.title: From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible
entries.summary: From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.
entries.content:
HistoryGlobal issues

From petitions to memes: How students made dissent visible

July 31, 2026

From imperial China to present-day India, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols of their age to challenge authority.

It was a clip destined to go viral.

On July 22, 2026, in rainy Mumbai, India, a casually dressed young woman stepped in front of a slow-moving police van carrying detained students. She placed her palm on the hood, forcing the vehicle to stop.

Mobile phones captured the moment from every angle. She too, raised her own phone and recorded the encounter. Within hours, the clip spread across India and beyond.

It became one of the defining visuals of the Cockroach Janta Party protests, a movement in which students demanded transparency and accountability, following leaks in India's medical entrance exams.

But the power of the moment lay not only in what she did, but in how quickly it was seen. A single gesture, a young woman confronting authority, became a symbol shared across millions of screens.

While the clip belongs to a generation raised on social media, the impulse behind it is much older.

From court petitions and revolutionary posters to photographs, umbrellas and memes, student movements have repeatedly adapted the tools and symbols available to them, turning them into vehicles for dissent.

Communicating dissent at court

Long before television or social media carried dissent across borders, students still found ways to make their grievances heard.

In Eastern Han China, for instance, scholars at the Imperial Academy (Taixue) aligned with reform-minded officials in opposing powerful eunuchs at court, whom many viewed as corrupt and politically overbearing.

They voiced their objections through public criticism, political networks and petitions.

In an era when political communication moved through official channels, petitions were among the established ways of bringing grievances before the throne. Written in formal language and delivered through the bureaucracy, they carried student concerns directly into the state's communication system.

Multiplying dissent through posters

Centuries later, communication and protest mechanisms evolved.

In Paris in 1968, students challenged university authorities and a conservative postwar social order. As demonstrations spread across the French capital and drew in workers, one of the movement's most enduring contributions emerged from a basement workshop at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts.

The Atelier Populaire ("People's Workshop") printed thousands of posters during the protests, many of them overnight. Their bold graphics, silhouettes and slogans became the visual language of the movement. Produced collectively, many carried no individual author's name, helping transform protest into a shared public voice.

The posters and their messages could appear in dozens of places overnight, giving the protest a wide local visual presence.

When a photograph became global witness

Protests also became more impactful when images could be transmitted across borders.

In Soweto in June 1976, Black South African students marched against the apartheid system's education policies, rejecting Afrikaans as a compulsory medium of instruction in Black schools. Many saw it as the language of an oppressive state and a barrier to equal education.

As thousands of students took to the streets, police opened fire. Amid the chaos, South African photographer Sam Nzima captured the image that would travel the world: 13-year-old Hector Pieterson being carried away from the scene after he was fatally shot.

The photograph became one of the defining images of apartheid. For many outside South Africa, it served as the lens through which the students' protest was seen and understood, helping build international awareness of and opposition to apartheid.

When images become iconic

In the spring of 1989, students gathered in Beijing's Tiananmen Square demanding democratic reforms, freedom of expression and an end to corruption. As the protests grew, so did the need for symbols that could communicate their message beyond the square.

In the final weeks of the occupation of Tiananmen Square, students built the Goddess of Democracy. Facing Mao Zedong's portrait, the 10-meter statue became a powerful symbol of the movement.

But while the students created one icon, history would produce another. After the brutal military crackdown on the protesters, a photograph of a lone man, later known as "Tank Man," standing facing a column of tanks traveled around the world.

Global media did not create these symbols, but amplified them. Cameras, newspapers and broadcasters transformed these local acts of defiance into enduring images of resistance.

From organizers to participants

Over time, protest communication no longer flowed only from organizers outward. Crowds and bystanders increasingly helped shape it.

In Chile in 2011, students demanding education reform used flash mobs, performances and public spectacle to draw attention to their cause. Protest was no longer just something people watched. It became something they could join.

In Hong Kong in 2014, students protesting Beijing's plans for electoral reform transformed everyday objects into political symbols. And what began as a practical response to pepper spray and tear gas soon became the defining image of the Umbrella Movement.

Modeled on Prague's original John Lennon Wall that was created after his murder in 1988 and went on to provide a space for people to express irritation with the communist regime, Lennon Walls in Hong Kong also became hubs of public expression, attracting thousands of people who left messages of support and protest on sticky notes attached to walls around the city.

From slur to symbol

And then there are the political platforms that shape which symbols become widely seen, as is the case in India recently.

Students protesting exam irregularities took an insult aimed at them and made it their own: "Cockroach" quickly became one of the movement's most recognizable symbols online.

Memes and reels often spread faster than official statements, with students using them to respond to criticism, mock their opponents and rally support.

Like posters in Paris or umbrellas in Hong Kong, this particular instance shows how memes can transform a disparaging label into a powerful protest symbol.

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

entries.title: Humanoid robots: Trump's latest China trade battle?
entries.summary: The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots, a market Chinese tech firms dominates. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Donald Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.
entries.content:
July 31, 2026

The US has banned foreign-made humanoid robots, a market Chinese tech firms dominates. Although Washington cited national security risks, analysts think Donald Trump is buying time for US robot makers to catch up.

In the latest sign of China's threat to the United States's tech dominance, the Trump administration on Tuesday banned new foreign-made humanoid and four-legged robotsfrom entering the country.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cited "unacceptable risks" to national security for the decision.

The FCC noted how the robots "collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots."

The move is widely seen as aimed squarely at China, which accounted for 85% of humanoid robot deployments last year, according to British bank Barclays.

How serious is the security threat from Chinese robots?

US officials warn that Chinese humanoid and quadruped (four-legged) robots can collect detailed location and personal data, be controlled remotely and pose risks for critical US infrastructure. Specific concerns center on the robots' potential dual-use — civilian and military purposes.

Unitree Robotics, a leading Chinese robot maker, appears on the Pentagon's list of firms with links to the Chinese military. Its robots have been used in army exercises.

Researchers have also shown that Unitree robots have security flaws that let attackers take control with a voice command and then use one robot to control others.

Washington is also concerned that a large cohort of low-cost Chinese robots could feed real-world data back to Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which are fast catching up with their US rivals.

The threat, however, is largely theoretical as most commercial humanoid robots are in early stages of development.

China has rejected the accusations, insisting the US is using national security as a pretext for protectionism to suppress Chinese technology. Beijing is expected to impose countermeasures, which could include curbs on the raw materials US robotics firms urgently need to scale up production.

The Trump administration has made no secret of its desire to help the domestic US robotics industry, which in turn supports the country's nearly trillion-dollar AI buildout. According to industry watchers, US President Donald Trump wants to ensure the likes of Figure AI, Tesla Optimus and Agility Robotics are protected from high-volume Chinese producers, whose robots often cost half the price or less of their US rivals.

Washington has put similar curbs on Chinese drones and solar panels and now levies a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles.

Will the ban help US robot makers catch up?

The ban is widely seen as Trump's attempt to buy time, having been caught off guard by how quickly China scaled robotics production.

According to Omdia, a tech research house, China has six firms in the Top 10 robotics rankings. Those firms shipped nearly 11,600 humanoids last year, versus a few hundred by US firms.

In March, Bank of America forecast around 90,000 shipments by the end of this year.

The US is widely seen as stronger at making a robot's brain smart through advanced AI, while China leads at mass-producing cheaper robots with bodies that move better thanks to high-performance actuators or robotic muscles.

Rush Doshi, director of the Initiative on China Strategy at the Council on Foreign Relations, described the ban as "one of the most significant actions taken so far in support of the US robotics ecosystem."

Evan Beard, CEO of Standard Bots, a maker of robot arms, thinks the Trump administration is sending an "unambiguous" message to China.

"Robotics is a technology America must lead and own — and foreign-subsidized robots will not be allowed to unfairly dominate US robotics..." Beard wrote on X.

Critics, however, think the ban could slow US AI innovation as researchers currently benefit from being able to run tests on budget-friendly Chinese robots.

"Restrictions can reduce security exposure, but they do not by themselves create a competitive domestic ecosystem," Georg Stieler, an advisor to the robotics industry, wrote on X.

CNBC, a US business television channel, cited Marc Einstein, a research director at Counterpoint Research, as saying the ban was "bad news for Chinese humanoid producers planning their IPOs in the coming months."

Einstein warned that Beijing could now "further restrict rare earth sales to American companies and … Chinese market access for American companies like Tesla and Nvidia."

How big could humanoid robots become?

Barclays estimates the market, currently worth just $2 to 3 billion (€1.7 to 2.6 billion), could reach $200 billion by 2035 in the most optimistic scenario, if the robot's brains, brawn and batteries can be improved.

Elon Musk is even more bullish, saying Tesla's Optimus could become "the biggest product ever" with long-term sales potentially reaching $10 trillion.

At scale, he believes the robots, which currently sell for about $100,000, could eventually cost $20,000 to $30,000 each — cheap enough for factories, warehouses and later homes.

Combining Barclays' forecast with Musk's target price points to roughly 7 to 10 million humanoid robots being sold each year by 2035.

In the near term, humanoids are expected to take on repetitive and physically demanding jobs in warehouses and factories. Later, they could expand into health, elderly care and household chores.

Edited by: Rob Mudge
